      Let \((\X,\B)\) denote a Borel space. Here we restrict attention to \(\X = \R^d\) (and write \(\|x\|\) for the Euclidean norm of \(x \in \X\)). Throughout let \(\pi(\cdot)\) be a finite `target' measure, and \(\pi(x)\) the corresponding Lebesgue density for some \(x \in \X\). We write \(P: \X \times \B \to [0,1]\) to denote a Markov transition kernel, meaning \(P(x,\cdot)\) is a probability measure for any \(x \in \X\) and \(P(\cdot,A)\) is measurable for any \(A \in \B\). \(P\) acts to the left on measures through \(\mu P(\cdot) := \int \mu(dx)P(x,dy)\) and to the right on functions through \(Pf(x) := \int f(y)P(x,dy)\). We let \(P^n(x,\cdot) := \int P^{n-1}(x,dy)P(y,\cdot)\) and say \(\pi(\cdot)\) is \emph{invariant} for \(P\) if \(\pi P(\cdot) = \pi(\cdot)\).

      Denote the Total Variation distance between two distributions \(\mu(\cdot)\) and \(\nu(\cdot)\) on \((\X,\B)\) as \(\|\mu(\cdot) - \nu(\cdot)\|_{TV} := \sup_{|f| \leq 1}|\mathbb{E}_\mu f - \mathbb{E}_\nu f|\). We say \(\pi(\cdot)\) is a \emph{limiting} distribution for \(P\) if \(\|P^n(x,\cdot) - \pi(\cdot)\|_{TV} \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\), for \(\pi\)-a.e. \(x \in \X\). Recall that an invariant distribution \(\pi(\cdot)\) will be the unique limiting measure if \(P\) is both \(\pi\)-irreducible and aperiodic.

      Consider a \(\pi\)-irreducible aperiodic Markov chain with state space \((\X,\B)\) and transition kernel \(P\). If there exists a \(\pi\)-a.e. finite \emph{Lyapunov} function \(V:\X \to [1,\infty]\) with `small' level sets, such that the condition \(PV(x) \leq \lambda V(x) + b\mathbbm{1}_{C_\omega}(x)\) holds for some \(\lambda < 1\), \(b<\infty\) and some set \(C_\omega:=\{x : V(x)\leq \omega\}\) with \(\omega<\infty\), then \(\exists \rho<1\) and a \(\pi\)-a.e. finite \(M:\X\to[0,\infty]\) such that
      \begin{equation} \label{eqn:geoerg}
      \|P^n(x,\cdot) - \pi(\cdot)\|_{TV} \leq M(x)\rho^n.
      \end{equation}
      The property whose failure is asserted below is \eqref{eqn:geoerg}, i.e. the existence of \(\rho<1\) and a \(\pi\)-a.e. finite \(M:\X\to[0,\infty]\) satisfying \eqref{eqn:geoerg} (geometric ergodicity of the chain). Recall that a set \(C \in \B\) is called `small' if there is a \(t<\infty\), a measure \(\nu(\cdot)\) defined on \((\X,\B)\) and an \(\epsilon>0\) such that \(\forall x \in C\) and \(\forall A \in \B\) it holds that \(P^t(x,A) \geq \epsilon \nu(A)\).

      We consider probability densities of the form \(\pi(x) \propto e^{-U(x)}\) for some \(U:\X \to [0,\infty)\). If we view \(U(x)= -\log\pi(x)\) as a `potential' energy in a physical system, it is natural to consider the larger phase space and construct the \emph{Hamiltonian}
      \begin{equation} \label{eqn:hamiltonian}
      H(x,p) = U(x) + \frac{1}{2}p^t M^{-1} p,
      \end{equation}
      where \(p\) denotes a \(d\)-dimensional `momentum' variable, \(M\) a \(d \times d\) `mass' matrix and \(p^t M^{-1}p/2\) the `kinetic' energy. Provided \(U(x)\) is differentiable, we can evolve the coordinates \((x_t,p_t)\) through time in such a way that \(H(x_t,p_t) = H(x_{t+s},p_{t+s})\) for any \(t,s \in \mathbb{R}\) using Hamilton's equations
      \begin{equation} \label{eqn:hamilton}
      \frac{d p_t}{dt} = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial x}, ~~ \frac{dx_t}{dt} = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p}.
      \end{equation}
      Solving \eqref{eqn:hamilton} results in \emph{Hamiltonian flow}. The standard choice when the Hamiltonian is of the form \eqref{eqn:hamiltonian} is the St\"{o}rmer--Verlet or \emph{leapfrog} scheme, in which \((x_{L\varepsilon},p_{L\varepsilon})\) is generated from \((x_0,p_0)\) using \(L\) steps of the recursion
      \begin{align*}
      p_{t+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}} &= p_t - \frac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla U(x_t), \\
      x_{t+\varepsilon} &= x_t + \varepsilon M^{-1}p_{t+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}, \\
      p_{t+\varepsilon} &= p_{t+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}} - \frac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla U(x_{t+\varepsilon}),
      \end{align*}
      for some step-size \(\varepsilon>0\). The resulting \emph{approximate} flow map \(\varphi_{L\varepsilon}(x_0,p_0) := (x_{L\varepsilon},p_{L\varepsilon})\) can be used as a proposal mechanism within the Metropolis--Hastings framework. Algorithm \ref{alg:hmc}: given \(x_{i-1}\), \(\varepsilon \geq 0\), \(\mathfrak{L}(\cdot)\), set \(x_0 \leftarrow x_{i-1}\), draw \(p_0 \sim N(0,M)\), \(L \sim \mathfrak{L}(\cdot)\), set \(T \leftarrow L\varepsilon\); draw \(u \sim U[0,1]\); set \(\delta \leftarrow H(x_0,p_0) - H\circ \varphi_T(x_0,p_0)\); if \(\log(u) < \delta\), set \(x_i \leftarrow \text{Pr}_x \circ \varphi_T(x_0,p_0)\), else set \(x_i \leftarrow x_{i-1}\).

      ### Definitions and notation used in Proof
      For fixed \(L\), let \(\mu_G(dp_0)\) denote the distribution \(N(0,I)\) from which \(p_0\) is drawn. The acceptance probability for the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo proposal is
      \[
      \alpha(x_0,x_{L\varepsilon})
      =
      1\wedge
      \frac{\pi(x_{L\varepsilon})}{\pi(x_0)}
      \exp\left(
      \frac12\|p_0\|^2-\frac12\|p_{L\varepsilon}\|^2
      \right),
      \]
      where \(1\wedge z=\min(1,z)\). The rejection probability is
      \[
      r(x_0)=1-\int \alpha(x_0,x_{L\varepsilon})\,\mu_G(dp_0).
      \]

      ### Proof
      Proof of Theorem 5.14.

      \begin{proof}
      Fix any \(\delta<1\). From [ref:R1],
      \[
       \sup_{\|p_0\|\leq\|x_0\|^\delta}
       \alpha(x_0,x_{L\varepsilon})\longrightarrow0
       \qquad\text{as }\|x_0\|\to\infty.
      \]
      Moreover,
      \[
       \mu_G\!\left(\left\{p_0:\|p_0\|>\|x_0\|^\delta\right\}\right)
       \longrightarrow0.
      \]
      Therefore, writing \(r(x_0)\) for the rejection probability as in [ref:R2],
      \begin{align*}
       1-r(x_0)
       &=\int\alpha(x_0,x_{L\varepsilon})\,\mu_G(dp_0)\\
       &\leq
       \sup_{\|p_0\|\leq\|x_0\|^\delta}
       \alpha(x_0,x_{L\varepsilon})
       +\mu_G\!\left(\left\{p_0:\|p_0\|>\|x_0\|^\delta\right\}\right)
       \longrightarrow0.
      \end{align*}
      This implies that the rejection probability \(r(x_0)\to1\) as \(\|x_0\|\to\infty\), and [ref:R3] then implies that the chain is not geometrically ergodic.
      \end{proof}

      When the number of leapfrog steps is drawn from a position-independent
      distribution \(\mathfrak{L}(\cdot)\) as in [ref:R4], the
      same conclusion follows provided the above argument is applied conditional on
      each fixed \(L\). For each fixed \(L\) the conditional acceptance probability
      tends to zero, while it is bounded by one. Since the law of \(L\) does not
      depend on \(x_0\), dominated convergence with respect to \(\mathfrak{L}(\cdot)\) shows that
      the unconditional acceptance probability also tends to zero.

      ##### Definitions and notation
      Let \(\X=\R^d\), and write \(\|x\|\) for the Euclidean norm of \(x\in\X\). Let \(\pi(\cdot)\) be the finite target measure, with Lebesgue density \(\pi(x)\) satisfying
      \[
      \pi(x)\propto e^{-U(x)},
      \]
      where \(U:\X\to[0,\infty)\) is differentiable and \(U(x)=-\log \pi(x)\). Write \(\nabla U(x)\) for the gradient of \(U\) at \(x\).

      Fix a leapfrog step size \(\varepsilon>0\), a fixed number \(L\ge 1\) of leapfrog steps, and fixed integration time \(T=L\varepsilon\). As in the source, take the mass matrix \(M=I\). The initial position is \(x_0\in\R^d\) and the initial momentum is \(p_0\in\R^d\); in the HMC algorithm \(p_0\sim N(0,I)\). The leapfrog recursion, with \(M=I\), is
      \[
      p_{t+\varepsilon/2}=p_t-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla U(x_t),\qquad
      x_{t+\varepsilon}=x_t+\varepsilon p_{t+\varepsilon/2},\qquad
      p_{t+\varepsilon}=p_{t+\varepsilon/2}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla U(x_{t+\varepsilon}),
      \]
      and the resulting approximate flow map is
      \[
      \varphi_{L\varepsilon}(x_0,p_0):=(x_{L\varepsilon},p_{L\varepsilon}).
      \]

      The candidate map is supplied as
      \[
      x_{L\varepsilon}
      =
      x_0-\frac{L\varepsilon^2}{2}\nabla U(x_0)
      -\varepsilon^2\sum_{i=1}^{L-1}(L-i)\nabla U(x_{i\varepsilon})
      +L\varepsilon p_0,
      \tag{9}
      \]
      where \(x_{i\varepsilon}\) denotes the position after \(i\) leapfrog steps.

      The final momentum is supplied as
      \[
      p_{L\varepsilon}
      =
      p_0-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla U(x_0)
      -\varepsilon\sum_{i=1}^{L-1}\nabla U(x_{i\varepsilon})
      -\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla U(x_{L\varepsilon}).
      \tag{11}
      \]

      The acceptance probability is
      \[
      \alpha(x_0,x_{L\varepsilon})
      =
      1\wedge
      \frac{\pi(x_{L\varepsilon})}{\pi(x_0)}
      \exp\left(
      \frac12\|p_0\|^2-\frac12\|p_{L\varepsilon}\|^2
      \right),
      \tag{10}
      \]
      where \(1\wedge z=\min(1,z)\).

      For \(\delta<1\), the constraint \(\|p_0\|\le \|x_0\|^\delta\) is imposed in the limit appearing in the lemma.

      ##### Assumptions

      \frac{\|\nabla U(x)\|}{\|x\|}

      \infty.
      \tag{17}

      - Condition (18) holds in the corrected form: there is a fixed \(C<\infty\) such that whenever

      \tag{18}

      \lim_{\substack{\|x_0\|\to\infty\\
      \|p_0\|\le \|x_0\|^\delta}}
      \alpha(x_0,x_{L\varepsilon})
      =
      0.
      \]

      ##### Definition 3.2
      ###### Definitions and notation
      Let \((\mathsf X,\mathcal B)\) be a Borel space; here \(\mathsf X=\mathbb R^d\), and \(\|x\|\) denotes the Euclidean norm of \(x\in\mathsf X\). Let \(\pi(\cdot)\) be a finite target measure with Lebesgue density \(\pi(x)\). Let \(P:\mathsf X\times\mathcal B\to[0,1]\) and \(Q:\mathsf X\times\mathcal B\to[0,1]\) be Markov transition kernels, so that \(P(x,\cdot)\) and \(Q(x,\cdot)\) are probability measures for each \(x\), and \(P(\cdot,A)\), \(Q(\cdot,A)\) are measurable for each \(A\in\mathcal B\). Let \(\delta_x(\cdot)\) denote the Dirac point mass at \(x\).

      If \(\pi(\cdot)\) and \(Q(x,\cdot)\) admit Lebesgue densities \(\pi(x)\) and \(q(x,y)\), define
      \[
      S:=\{(x,y)\in\mathsf X^2:\pi(x)q(x,y)>0\}.
      \]
      For \((x,y)\in S\), set
      \begin{equation}
      r(x,y):=\frac{\pi(y)q(y,x)}{\pi(x)q(x,y)},
      \tag{eqn:accept}
      \end{equation}
      and set \(r(x,y):=0\) otherwise. Then the acceptance probability is
      \[
      \alpha(x,y):=1\wedge r(x,y).
      \]
      Here \(r(x,y)\) is the two-argument Metropolis–Hastings ratio, distinct from the one-argument rejection probability \(r(x)\) appearing in the definition below.

      ###### Assumptions
      No additional assumptions are imposed beyond those internal to the definition: \(Q\) is a Markov kernel and \(\alpha(x,y)\) is defined as above via `(eqn:accept)`, which presupposes that \(\pi(\cdot)\) and \(Q(x,\cdot)\) admit the Lebesgue densities \(\pi(x)\) and \(q(x,y)\).

      ###### Statement
      **Definition 3.2.** We say that \(P\) is of the *Metropolis–Hastings* type if
      \begin{equation}
      P(x,dy)=\alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy)+r(x)\delta_x(dy),
      \tag{eqn:mhtype}
      \end{equation}
      where \(Q\) is a Markov kernel, \(\alpha(x,y)\) is defined in `(eqn:accept)`, and
      \[
      r(x)=1-\int \alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy).
      \]

      ##### Definitions and notation
      Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal B)$ denote a Borel space; here $\mathcal X=\mathbb R^d$ and $\|x\|$ denotes the Euclidean norm of $x\in\mathcal X$. Throughout, $\pi(\cdot)$ is a finite “target” measure and $\pi(x)$ the corresponding Lebesgue density for $x\in\mathcal X$. We write $P:\mathcal X\times\mathcal B\to[0,1]$ for a Markov transition kernel, meaning $P(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure for any $x\in\mathcal X$ and $P(\cdot,A)$ is measurable for any $A\in\mathcal B$. $P$ acts to the left on measures through $\mu P(\cdot):=\int\mu(dx)P(x,dy)$ and to the right on functions through $Pf(x):=\int f(y)P(x,dy)$. We let $P^n(x,\cdot):=\int P^{n-1}(x,dy)P(y,\cdot)$ and say $\pi(\cdot)$ is *invariant* for $P$ if $\pi P(\cdot)=\pi(\cdot)$.

      The Total Variation distance between two distributions $\mu(\cdot)$ and $\nu(\cdot)$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal B)$ is
      \[
      \|\mu(\cdot)-\nu(\cdot)\|_{TV}:=\sup_{|f|\leq 1}\bigl|\mathbb E_\mu f-\mathbb E_\nu f\bigr|.
      \]
      $\pi(\cdot)$ is a *limiting* distribution for $P$ if $\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi(\cdot)\|_{TV}\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ for $\pi$-a.e. $x\in\mathcal X$.

      The property whose failure is asserted is
      \begin{equation} \label{eqn:geoerg}
      \|P^n(x,\cdot) - \pi(\cdot)\|_{TV} \leq M(x)\rho^n,
      \end{equation}
      i.e.\ existence of $\rho<1$ and a $\pi$-a.e.\ finite $M:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty]$ satisfying \eqref{eqn:geoerg} (geometric ergodicity of the chain).

      *Metropolis--Hastings type kernel.* We say $P$ is of the *Metropolis--Hastings* type if
      \begin{equation} \label{eqn:mhtype}
      P(x,dy) = \alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy) + r(x)\delta_x(dy),
      \end{equation}
      where $Q$ is a Markov kernel, $\alpha(x,y)$ is defined in \eqref{eqn:accept} and
      \[
      r(x) = 1- \int \alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy).
      \]

      *Candidate kernel and acceptance probability.* A candidate transition kernel is induced as $Q(x,A)=\int\mathbbm{1}_A(g_\xi(x))\mu(d\xi)$ for any $A\in\mathcal B$, from a family $\{g_\xi,\xi\in\Xi\}$ of “candidate” maps with $\xi\sim\mu(\cdot)$. If $\pi(\cdot)$ and $Q(x,\cdot)$ admit densities $\pi(x)$ and $q(x,y)$, let $S:=\{(x,y)\in\mathcal X^2:\pi(x)q(x,y)>0\}$; then for $(x,y)\in S$ set
      \begin{equation} \label{eqn:accept}
      r(x,y) := \frac{\pi(y)q(y,x)}{\pi(x)q(x,y)},
      \end{equation}
      and set $r(x,y):=0$ otherwise, and then $\alpha(x,y):=1\wedge r(x,y)$ (the “acceptance probability” $\alpha:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to[0,1]$).

      ##### Assumptions
      \begin{enumerate}
      \item[(i)] $P$ is of Metropolis--Hastings type: there is a Markov kernel $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal B)$ such that
      \[
      P(x,dy) = \alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy) + r(x)\delta_x(dy),
      \]
      with $\alpha(x,y)=1\wedge r(x,y)$ given by \eqref{eqn:accept} (and $r(x,y)=0$ off $S$), and
      \[
      r(x) = 1- \int \alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy).
      \]
      \item[(ii)] $\mathrm{esssup}\, r(x) = 1$.
      \end{enumerate}

      ##### Statement
      If $P$ is of Metropolis--Hastings type, then \eqref{eqn:geoerg}, namely
      \[
      \|P^n(x,\cdot) - \pi(\cdot)\|_{TV} \leq M(x)\rho^n,
      \]
      *fails* to hold if $\mathrm{esssup}\, r(x) = 1$.

### HMC setup

- State space: \(\mathcal X=\mathbb R^d\), with Euclidean norm \(\|\cdot\|\).
- Target: a finite measure \(\pi\) with Lebesgue density \(\pi(x)\propto e^{-U(x)}\), where \(U:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)\) is differentiable and \(\nabla U\) is its gradient.
- Mass matrix: \(M=I\), hence momentum \(p_0\sim N(0,I)\) and kinetic energy \(\frac12\|p\|^2\).
- Step size \(\varepsilon>0\), fixed positive integer \(L\ge1\), integration time \(T=L\varepsilon\). The sums \(\sum_{i=1}^{L-1}\) are empty when \(L=1\).
- Leapfrog recursion:
  \[
  p_{t+\varepsilon/2}=p_t-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla U(x_t),\qquad
  x_{t+\varepsilon}=x_t+\varepsilon p_{t+\varepsilon/2},\qquad
  p_{t+\varepsilon}=p_{t+\varepsilon/2}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla U(x_{t+\varepsilon}),
  \]
  with \(\varphi_{L\varepsilon}(x_0,p_0)=(x_{L\varepsilon},p_{L\varepsilon})\).
- Acceptance probability:
  \[
  \alpha(x_0,x_{L\varepsilon})
  =
  1\wedge
  \frac{\pi(x_{L\varepsilon})}{\pi(x_0)}
  \exp\left(
  \frac12\|p_0\|^2-\frac12\|p_{L\varepsilon}\|^2
  \right).
  \]
- Rejection probability:
  \[
  r(x_0)=1-\int\alpha(x_0,x_{L\varepsilon})\,\mu_G(dp_0),
  \]
  where \(\mu_G\) is the law \(N(0,I)\) of \(p_0\).

### Markov-chain and ergodicity notation

- \(P,Q\) are Markov transition kernels on \((\mathcal X,\mathcal B)\).
- TV distance:
  \[
  \|\mu-\nu\|_{TV}:=\sup_{|f|\le1}\left|\mathbb E_\mu f-\mathbb E_\nu f\right|,
  \]
  with no extra \(1/2\) factor.
- The geometric-ergodicity display is
  \[
  \|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi(\cdot)\|_{TV}\le M(x)\rho^n
  \tag{eqn:geoerg}
  \]
  for some \(\rho<1\) and \(\pi\)-a.e. finite \(M:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty]\). The source writes the display without spelling out the quantifier over \(n\), but the intended bound is over iteration counts \(n\).
- Metropolis–Hastings type and the distinction between the two-argument ratio \(r(x,y)\) and the one-argument rejection probability \(r(x)\) are as in R2.
- The source additionally recalls a Lyapunov/minorization sufficient condition for geometric ergodicity and the definition of small sets; these are background and are not independently invoked by the selected proof, which instead uses R3 to rule out geometric ergodicity.

### Hypotheses (17)–(19)

- Condition (17):
  \[
  \lim_{\|x\|\to\infty}\frac{\|\nabla U(x)\|}{\|x\|}=\infty.
  \]
  This is a genuine limit to \(+\infty\), not an \(O\) or \(o\) statement.

- Condition (18), corrected form:
  there is \(C<\infty\) such that for all \(x,y\),
  \[
  \|y\|\ge3\|x\|\ge C
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \|\nabla U(y)\|\ge3\|\nabla U(x)\|.
  \]
  This is not the superseded printed version with \(\|y\|\ge2\|x\|\).

- Condition (19):
  \[
  \lim_{\substack{\|x\|\to\infty\\ \|y\|\ge2^L\|x\|}}
  \left(
  U(x)-U(y)-\frac12\|x\|^2
  \right)
  =
  -\infty.

\[
S:=\{(x,y)\in\mathsf X^2:\pi(x)q(x,y)>0\}.
\]
For \((x,y)\in S\), set
\[
r(x,y):=\frac{\pi(y)q(y,x)}{\pi(x)q(x,y)},
\tag{eqn:accept}
\]
and set \(r(x,y):=0\) otherwise. The acceptance probability is
\[
\alpha(x,y):=1\wedge r(x,y).
\]

\[
P(x,dy)=\alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy)+r(x)\delta_x(dy),
\tag{eqn:mhtype}
\]
where \(Q\) is a Markov kernel, \(\alpha(x,y)\) is defined as above, and
\[
r(x)=1-\int \alpha(x,y)Q(x,dy).
\]

\lim_{\|x\|\to\infty}\frac{\|\nabla U(x)\|}{\|x\|}=\infty.
\tag{17}
\]

\[
\|p_0\|\le \|x_0\|^\delta,
\]
the leapfrog iterates satisfy
\[
\|x_{i\varepsilon}\|\ge 3\|x_{(i-1)\varepsilon}\|,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,L,
\tag{eq:stepwiseexpansion}
\]
and therefore
\[
\|x_{L\varepsilon}\|\ge 3^L\|x_0\|.
\tag{eq:3Lexpansion}
\]

Let \(X\) be a Polish space and let \(\mu\) be a finite Borel measure on \(X\). Then \(\mu\) is regular: for every Borel set \(B\subseteq X\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist a closed set \(F\subseteq B\) and an open set \(G\supseteq B\) such that
\[
\mu(B\setminus F)<\varepsilon,
\qquad
\mu(G\setminus B)<\varepsilon.
\]
Consequently, if \(A\) is \(\mu\)-measurable and \(\mu(A)=0\), then there exists a Borel set \(N\supseteq A\) with \(\mu(N)=0\). Indeed, by outer regularity one may choose open sets \(G_n\supseteq A\) with \(\mu(G_n)<1/n\), and then \(N=\bigcap_{n\ge1}G_n\) is a Borel null set containing \(A\).
